topic: Wire antennas, arrays, Yagis and loading

notes.front: What is a phased array?
notes.back: An antenna of several driven elements, connected through phasing lines, whose phase relationships control the radiation pattern.
notes.explanation: The pool gives controlling the radiation pattern as the purpose of connecting multiple driven elements this way.
notes.example: Like two loudspeakers playing the same note: timing decides where their sound reinforces and where it cancels.
notes.evidence: E9E11 (A) What is the purpose of using multiple driven elements connected through phasing lines? A. To control the antenna’s radiation pattern

notes.front: What is a cardioid pattern?
notes.back: A heart-shaped radiation pattern. Two 1/4-wavelength verticals spaced 1/4 wavelength apart and fed 90 degrees out of phase produce one.
notes.explanation: The pair's spacing and phase difference together decide the shape, as the pool's question sets them out.
notes.example: Like a microphone that hears well in front and to the sides, but hardly at all from directly behind.
notes.evidence: E9C02 (A) What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/4- wavelength apart and fed 90 degrees out of phase? A. Cardioid

notes.front: What is a long-wire antenna?
notes.back: An antenna that is a wavelength or longer at the operating frequency.
notes.explanation: Its length in wavelengths, not any special shape, is what makes it a long wire.
notes.example: Like a random-wire antenna, but deliberately at least one full wavelength long.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, long-wire antenna, p. 4-41
notes.evidence: A LONG-WIRE ANTENNA is an antenna that is a wavelength or longer at the operating frequency.

notes.front: What is a rhombic antenna?
notes.back: Four long conductors joined in a rhombus (diamond) shape, terminated by a noninductive resistor to give a unidirectional pattern.
notes.explanation: The Navy course calls it the highest development of the long-wire antenna.
notes.example: Like four long wires strung between four poles to form a flat diamond, with a resistor across the far corner.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, rhombic antenna, p. 4-42
notes.evidence: The highest development of the long-wire antenna is the RHOMBIC ANTENNA (see figure 4-37). It consists of four conductors joined to form a rhombus, or diamond shape. The antenna is placed end to end and terminated by a noninductive resistor to produce a uni-directional pattern.

notes.front: What is an off-center-fed dipole (OCFD)?
notes.back: A dipole fed between its centre and one end instead of at the midpoint, to give a similar feed-point impedance on several bands.
notes.explanation: The pool gives a similar feed-point impedance on several bands as the purpose, not lobe suppression or a wider resonance.
notes.example: Like an ordinary wire dipole, but with the feed line attached a third of the way along instead of in the middle.
notes.evidence: E9C05 (A) What is the purpose of feeding an off-center-fed dipole (OCFD) between the center and one end instead of at the midpoint? A. To create a similar feed point impedance on multiple bands

notes.front: What is a folded dipole?
notes.back: An ordinary half-wave dipole with one or more extra conductors connected across its ends, parallel to it and closely spaced.
notes.explanation: The Navy course spaces the extra conductors a very small fraction of a wavelength away; several inches is common.
notes.example: Like a long, thin loop of wire: the dipole and its parallel partner joined at both ends.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, folded dipole, p. 4-24
notes.evidence: A FOLDED DIPOLE is an ordinary half-wave antenna that has one or more additional conductors connected across its ends. Additional conductors are mounted parallel to the dipole elements at a distance equal to a very small fraction of a wavelength. Spacing of several inches is common.

notes.front: What is a G5RV antenna?
notes.back: A wire antenna centre-fed through a specific length of open-wire line, which connects through a coupling device to coaxial feed line.
notes.explanation: The pool specifies a particular length of open-wire line between the wire and the coax.
notes.example: Like a centre-fed wire dipole, but with a set length of ladder line hanging from its centre before the coax begins.
notes.evidence: A. A wire antenna center-fed through a specific length of open-wire line connected to a balun and coaxial feed line

notes.front: What is a balun, as the pool uses it in a G5RV?
notes.back: The device joining two different feed lines: the G5RV's open-wire line connects to it, and it connects to the coaxial feed line.
notes.explanation: The name is short for balanced/unbalanced: a US space-agency paper describes baluns as RF balanced/unbalanced transformers used to match impedances. The pool also mentions a 4:1 balun, so they come in different ratios.
notes.example: Like an adaptor between two kinds of cable, placed where ladder line meets coax.
notes.source: NASA NTRS 20120008524, "Calibration Procedure for Measuring S-Parameters in Balun Applications on 150-ohm High-Speed Cables"
notes.evidence: we utilize RF balanced/unbalanced transformers (called baluns for short), which are primarily used to match the impedance

notes.front: What is a Zepp antenna?
notes.back: An end-fed half-wavelength dipole.
notes.explanation: It is still a half-wave dipole; what sets it apart is being fed at one end instead of the centre.
notes.example: Like a half-wave dipole with the feed moved from the middle to one tip.
notes.evidence: E9C10 (B) Which of the following describes a Zepp antenna? A. A horizontal array capable of quickly changing the direction of maximum radiation by changing phasing lines B. An end-fed half-wavelength dipole

notes.front: What is an extended double Zepp?
notes.back: A centre-fed dipole antenna 1.25 wavelengths long.
notes.explanation: Unlike the plain Zepp, it is fed in the centre, and it is longer than a half wave.
notes.example: Like a centre-fed dipole stretched to one and a quarter wavelengths.
notes.evidence: E9C12 (C) Which of the following describes an extended double Zepp antenna? A. An end-fed full-wave dipole antenna B. A center-fed 1.5-wavelength dipole antenna C. A center-fed 1.25-wavelength dipole antenna

notes.front: What is a parabolic reflector antenna?
notes.back: A dish antenna; an ideal one gains 6 dB each time the operating frequency is doubled.
notes.explanation: Its gain rises with frequency, as the pool's question on doubling the frequency shows.
notes.example: Like a converted satellite television dish, used as an amateur microwave antenna.
notes.evidence: E9D01 (D) How much does the gain of an ideal parabolic reflector antenna increase when the operating frequency is doubled? A. 2 dB B. 3 dB C. 4 dB D. 6 dB

notes.front: What is a parasitic element?
notes.back: An element placed near the driven element, close enough for coupling, that gets its power from the driven element.
notes.explanation: It is not wired to the transmitter; the energy reaches it through coupling from the driven element.
notes.example: Like the reflector and directors of a Yagi: only the driven element is connected to the feed line.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, array antennas, definition of terms, p. 4-25
notes.evidence: A PARASITIC ELEMENT is located near the driven element from which it gets its power. It is placed close enough to the driven element to permit coupling.

notes.front: What is a loading coil?
notes.back: An inductor added in series with an electrically short antenna, whose inductive reactance cancels the antenna's capacitive reactance.
notes.explanation: A too-short antenna is resonant above the operating frequency, so it offers capacitive reactance; lumped inductive reactance compensates.
notes.example: Like the coil wound on a short mobile HF whip so that it can resonate on a low band.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, antenna loading, p. 4-18
notes.evidence: If the antenna is too short for the wavelength being used, it is resonant at a higher frequency than that at which it is being excited. Therefore, it offers a capacitive reactance at the excitation frequency. This capacitive reactance can be compensated for by introducing a lumped-inductive reactance

notes.front: What is an antenna's SWR bandwidth?
notes.back: The range of frequencies over which the antenna keeps a usable SWR; it narrows as the antenna's Q increases.
notes.explanation: The pool links it to Q: as antenna Q rises, SWR bandwidth decreases.
notes.example: Like a tuned circuit's passband: a sharp, high-Q antenna matches well over only a small slice of a band.
notes.evidence: E9D08 (B) What happens as the Q of an antenna increases? A. SWR bandwidth increases B. SWR bandwidth decreases

notes.front: What is top loading of a short vertical?
notes.back: Loading an electrically short vertical at its top; the pool credits it with improved radiation efficiency.
notes.explanation: The pool names improved radiation efficiency, not lower Q or strength, as its advantage for a short HF vertical.
notes.example: Like fitting a capacitance hat of spokes at the top of a short whip.
notes.evidence: E9D07 (D) What is an advantage of top loading an electrically short HF vertical antenna? A. Lower Q B. Greater structural strength C. Higher losses D. Improved radiation efficiency

notes.front: Two verticals are 1/4 wavelength apart and fed 90 degrees apart in phase. Why is there no radiation in one direction along the line joining them?
notes.back: In that direction the quarter-cycle travel delay adds to the quarter-cycle feed difference, so the two fields are 180 degrees apart and cancel.
notes.explanation: The Navy course works it through: a quarter cycle of travel plus a quarter cycle of feed difference makes exactly 180 degrees.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, phasing, p. 4-26
notes.evidence: Radiation from antenna 2 toward receiving location Y will reach antenna 1 after 1/4 cycle. The energy in antenna 1 was 1/4 cycle behind that of antenna 2 to begin with; therefore, the radiation from antenna 1 toward receiving point Y will be exactly 180 degrees out of phase with that of antenna 2.

notes.front: When waves from two elements reach a distant point, what happens if they arrive in phase, and if they arrive out of phase?
notes.back: In phase they add, giving a stronger signal; out of phase they cancel, reducing it.
notes.explanation: Whether the components add or cancel depends on their phase where they meet.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, phasing, p. 4-26
notes.evidence: If the different components arrive at a given point in the same phase, they add, making a stronger signal available. If they arrive out of phase, they cancel, reducing the signal strength.

notes.front: In an end-fire array, where is the principal direction of radiation?
notes.back: Along the plane of the array and perpendicular to the elements: out of the ends of the array.
notes.explanation: The Navy course says radiation comes from the end of the array, which is how the arrangement got its name.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, array antennas, definition of terms, p. 4-25
notes.evidence: An END-FIRE ARRAY is one in which the principal direction of radiation is along the plane of the array and perpendicular to the elements. Radiation is from the end of the array, which is the reason this arrangement is referred to as an end-fire array.

notes.front: The currents in the elements of an end-fire array are usually {{c1::180 degrees}} out of phase with each other.
notes.back: 180 degrees
notes.explanation: Adjacent elements carry opposite currents, as the arrows in the course's figure show.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, end-fire arrays, p. 4-33
notes.evidence: The currents in the elements of the end-fire array, however, are usually 180 degrees out of phase with each other as indicated by the arrows.

notes.front: Two 1/4-wavelength verticals are 1/2 wavelength apart. How does their pattern change between feeding them in phase and 180 degrees out of phase?
notes.back: In phase: a figure-eight broadside to the array's axis. 180 degrees out of phase: a figure-eight along the axis.
notes.explanation: The pool pairs these two cases: in-phase feed keys the broadside figure-eight, and 180-degree feed the end-fire one.
notes.evidence: E9C03 (C) What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/2- wavelength apart and fed in phase? A. Omni-directional B. Cardioid C. A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array

notes.front: You want two 1/4-wavelength verticals to favour one direction, with little radiation to the rear. Which arrangement does that?
notes.choices:
A) Spaced 1/4 wavelength, fed 90 degrees out of phase
B) Spaced 1/2 wavelength, fed in phase
C) Spaced 1/2 wavelength, fed 180 degrees out of phase
D) Spaced 1/2 wavelength, fed 90 degrees out of phase
notes.back: Spaced 1/4 wavelength, fed 90 degrees out of phase
notes.choicesExplained: B: in-phase feed at half-wave spacing gives a broadside figure-eight, two directions. C: 180-degree feed gives an end-fire figure-eight, also two directions. D: the pool pairs the 90-degree feed with quarter-wave spacing, not half-wave.
notes.explanation: Quarter-wave spacing with a 90-degree feed difference gives the cardioid, which favours one side.
notes.evidence: E9C02 (A) What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/4- wavelength apart and fed 90 degrees out of phase? A. Cardioid

notes.front: What kind of pattern does a long-wire antenna have, according to the Navy course?
notes.back: Directional patterns that are sharp in both the horizontal and vertical planes, concentrating radiation at low vertical angles.
notes.explanation: The course lists this among the long wire's advantages, alongside simple construction.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, long-wire antenna, p. 4-41
notes.evidence: Another factor is that long-wire antennas have directional patterns that are sharp in both the horizontal and vertical planes. Also, they tend to concentrate the radiation at the low vertical angles.

notes.front: Over what frequency range does a long-wire antenna work well, in the Navy course?
notes.back: Up to twice the frequency it was cut for; it radiates efficiently wherever its length is at least about 1/2 wavelength.
notes.explanation: It also accepts power efficiently on lower frequencies, down to where it is only about half a wavelength long.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, long-wire antenna, p. 4-41
notes.evidence: The long-wire antenna will work well and give satisfactory gain and directivity over a frequency range up to twice the value for which it was cut. In addition, it will accept power and radiate it efficiently on any frequency for which its overall length is not less than approximately 1/2 wavelength.

notes.front: How can a rhombic antenna be made from V antennas?
notes.back: Two obtuse-angle V antennas placed side by side in a horizontal plane, terminated so the antenna is nonresonant and unidirectional.
notes.explanation: The termination is what turns the pair into a nonresonant, one-way antenna.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, rhombic antenna, p. 4-42
notes.evidence: A rhombic antenna can be made of two obtuse-angle V antennas that are placed side by side, erected in a horizontal plane, and terminated so the antenna is nonresonant and unidirectional.

notes.front: What are two advantages of a rhombic antenna, according to the Navy course?
notes.back: It is useful over a wide frequency range, and it is easier to build and maintain than other antennas of comparable gain and directivity.
notes.explanation: Its gain, directivity and impedance change with frequency, but by amounts small enough to be neglected.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, rhombic antenna, advantages, p. 4-43
notes.evidence: The rhombic antenna is useful over a wide frequency range. Although some changes in gain, directivity, and characteristic impedance do occur with a change in operating frequency, these changes are small enough to be neglected. The rhombic antenna is much easier to construct and maintain than other antennas of comparable gain and directivity.

notes.front: What is a practical drawback of a high-frequency rhombic antenna?
notes.back: Its wires are several hundred feet long, so it is used only where a large plot of land is available.
notes.explanation: Each leg is at least 1 or 2 wavelengths long at the lowest frequency, and 8 to 12 wavelengths where more gain is wanted.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, rhombic antenna, disadvantages, p. 4-44
notes.evidence: Each leg is made at least 1 or 2 wavelengths long at the lowest operating frequency. When increased gain and directivity are required, legs of from 8 to 12 wavelengths are used. These requirements mean that high-frequency rhombic antennas have wires of several hundred feet in length. Therefore, they are used only when a large plot of land is available.

notes.front: How does a folded dipole's feed-point impedance depend on the number of conductors?
notes.back: It rises as the square of the number of conductors: a three-wire folded dipole has nine times a simple dipole's impedance.
notes.explanation: Two conductors therefore give four times the simple centre-fed dipole's impedance.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, folded dipole, p. 4-24
notes.evidence: In any folded dipole, the increase of impedance is the square of the number of conductors used in the radiator. Thus, a three-wire dipole has nine times

notes.front: You build a folded dipole from four parallel conductors. How does its feed-point impedance compare with a simple centre-fed dipole's?
notes.choices:
A) 16 times as high
B) 4 times as high
C) 8 times as high
D) The same
notes.back: 16 times as high
notes.choicesExplained: B: four times is the two-wire case. C: eight times doubles instead of squaring. D: the extra conductors do raise the impedance.
notes.explanation: The increase is the square of the number of conductors, and 4 squared is 16.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, folded dipole, p. 4-24
notes.evidence: In any folded dipole, the increase of impedance is the square of the number of conductors used in the radiator.

notes.front: How does a folded dipole compare with a simple dipole for pattern and frequency range?
notes.back: Same directional characteristics, but its reactance changes more slowly away from resonance, so it works over a much wider frequency range.
notes.explanation: The slower change of reactance with frequency is the reason the course gives for the wider range.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, folded dipole, p. 4-24
notes.evidence: The directional characteristics of a folded dipole are the same as those of a simple dipole. However, the reactance of a folded dipole varies much more slowly as the frequency is varied from resonance. Because of this the folded dipole can be used over a much wider frequency range than is possible with a simple dipole.

notes.front: Why does the Navy course use a folded dipole in place of a centre-fed half-wave radiator in arrays with parasitic elements?
notes.back: Parasitic elements and stacking lower the radiation resistance and make matching difficult; a folded dipole overcomes this.
notes.explanation: The course names the problem, a lower radiation resistance that is hard to match, and the folded dipole as a convenient way round it.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, folded dipole, p. 4-24
notes.evidence: The use of parasitic elements and various stacking arrangements causes a reduction in the radiation resistance of a center-fed, half-wave antenna. Under these conditions obtaining a proper impedance match between the radiator and the transmission line is often difficult. A convenient method of overcoming these difficulties is to use a FOLDED DIPOLE in place of the center-fed radiator.

notes.front: You raise a horizontal dipole from 1/4 wavelength to 1 wavelength above ground. What happens to the takeoff angle of its lowest elevation lobe?
notes.choices:
A) It decreases
B) It increases
C) It stays the same
D) The lobe disappears
notes.back: It decreases
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the reverse of what the pool keys. C: height does change the elevation pattern. D: the lowest lobe remains; it moves nearer the horizon.
notes.explanation: For a horizontally polarized antenna, more height lowers the takeoff angle of the lowest elevation lobe.
notes.evidence: E9C13 (B) How does the radiation pattern of a horizontally polarized antenna vary with increasing height above ground? A. The takeoff angle of the lowest elevation lobe increases B. The takeoff angle of the lowest elevation lobe decreases

notes.front: An ideal parabolic reflector is used at four times its original frequency. How much does its gain rise?
notes.choices:
A) 12 dB
B) 6 dB
C) 24 dB
D) 4 dB
notes.back: 12 dB
notes.choicesExplained: B: 6 dB is one doubling; four times the frequency is two doublings. C: 24 dB adds 6 dB for each unit of the factor of four. D: 4 dB confuses the factor with decibels.
notes.explanation: Each doubling of frequency adds 6 dB to an ideal dish's gain; two doublings add 12 dB.
notes.evidence: E9D01 (D) How much does the gain of an ideal parabolic reflector antenna increase when the operating frequency is doubled? A. 2 dB B. 3 dB C. 4 dB D. 6 dB

notes.front: How is an antenna that is too long for the frequency loaded, compared with one that is too short?
notes.back: Too long: it looks inductive, so series capacitive reactance is added. Too short: it looks capacitive, so series inductance is added.
notes.explanation: In each case the added reactance is the opposite kind, so it cancels the antenna's own.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, antenna loading, p. 4-18
notes.evidence: Similarly, if the antenna is too long for the transmitting frequency, it offers an inductive reactance. Inductive reactance can be compensated for by introducing a lumped-capacitive reactance

notes.front: A 7 MHz mobile whip is far shorter than a quarter wavelength. What reactance does it show at 7 MHz, and what is added to cancel it?
notes.back: Capacitive reactance, cancelled by the inductive reactance of a loading coil.
notes.explanation: A too-short antenna is resonant above the frequency in use, so it offers capacitive reactance, which lumped inductive reactance compensates.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, antenna loading, p. 4-18
notes.evidence: If the antenna is too short for the wavelength being used, it is resonant at a higher frequency than that at which it is being excited. Therefore, it offers a capacitive reactance at the excitation frequency.

notes.front: You replace a full-size 40 m quarter-wave vertical with a short whip resonated by a loading coil. What happens to the SWR bandwidth?
notes.choices:
A) It decreases
B) It increases
C) It is unchanged if the coil is at the feed point
D) It is unchanged if the coil is at a voltage maximum
notes.back: It decreases
notes.choicesExplained: B: loading narrows the bandwidth. C and D: the pool gives no coil position that leaves it unchanged.
notes.explanation: Resonating an electrically short antenna with loading coils decreases its SWR bandwidth.
notes.evidence: E9D06 (B) What happens to SWR bandwidth when one or more loading coils are used to resonate an electrically short antenna? A. It is increased B. It is decreased

notes.front: What happens as more parasitic elements are added to a Yagi?
notes.back: Gain generally rises, but the frequency response and beamwidth both become narrower.
notes.explanation: The Navy course adds that proper adjustment of such an antenna is therefore critical.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, parasitic arrays, p. 4-39
notes.evidence: In general, the greater number of parasitic elements used, the greater the gain. However, a greater number of such elements causes the array to have a narrower frequency response as well as a narrower beamwidth. Therefore, proper adjustment of the antenna is critical.

notes.front: In the Navy course, how much gain do extra directors add to a three-element Yagi?
notes.back: Three elements give about 5 dB; one more director adds 2 dB, and further directors have less and less effect.
notes.explanation: Gain does not grow in step with the number of elements.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, parasitic arrays, p. 4-39
notes.evidence: The gain does not increase directly with the number of elements used. For example, a three-element Yagi array has a relative power gain of 5 dB. Adding another director results in a 2 dB increase. Additional directors have less and less effect.

notes.front: What sets the power gain and directivity of a parasitic array?
notes.back: The lengths of the parasitic elements and the spacing between them.
notes.explanation: Neither decides it alone: gain and directivity depend on the two together.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, summary, p. 4-56
notes.evidence: The amount of power gain and directivity depends on the lengths of the parasitic elements and the spacing between them.

notes.front: How does a director differ from a reflector in a parasitic array?
notes.back: A director radiates away from the driven element; a reflector radiates toward it.
notes.explanation: Both are parasitic elements; the direction each radiates relative to the driven element decides which it is.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 10, chapter 4, parasitic arrays, p. 4-36
notes.evidence: When the parasitic element is placed so that it radiates away from the driven element, the element is a director. When the parasitic element is placed so that it radiates toward the driven element, the parasitic element is a reflector.

notes.front: How does a Zepp antenna differ from an extended double Zepp?
notes.back: A Zepp is an end-fed half-wavelength dipole; an extended double Zepp is a centre-fed dipole 1.25 wavelengths long.
notes.explanation: They differ in both feed point (end or centre) and length (a half or one and a quarter wavelengths).
notes.evidence: E9C12 (C) Which of the following describes an extended double Zepp antenna? A. An end-fed full-wave dipole antenna B. A center-fed 1.5-wavelength dipole antenna C. A center-fed 1.25-wavelength dipole antenna

notes.front: What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/2-wavelength apart and fed 180 degrees out of phase?
notes.choices:
A) Cardioid
B) Omni-directional
C) A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array
D) A figure-eight oriented along the axis of the array
notes.back: A figure-eight oriented along the axis of the array
notes.choicesExplained: A: a cardioid comes from quarter-wave spacing with a 90-degree phase difference. B: two spaced, phased verticals are directional, not omnidirectional. C: the broadside figure-eight is the in-phase case.
notes.explanation: The Navy course's end-fire example is this arrangement: two elements half a wavelength apart fed 180 degrees out of phase, radiating along the line of the array.
notes.evidence: wavelength apart and fed 180 degrees out of phase? A. Cardioid B. Omni-directional C. A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array D. A figure-eight oriented along the axis of the array

notes.front: What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/4-wavelength apart and fed 90 degrees out of phase?
notes.choices:
A) Cardioid
B) A figure-eight end-fire along the axis of the array
C) A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array
D) Omni-directional
notes.back: Cardioid
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: figure-eights come from half-wave spacing. D: the phasing makes the pair directional, not omnidirectional.
notes.explanation: Quarter-wave spacing plus a 90-degree feed difference makes the signals add towards one side and cancel towards the other.
notes.evidence: wavelength apart and fed 90 degrees out of phase? A. Cardioid

notes.front: What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/2-wavelength apart and fed in phase?
notes.choices:
A) Omni-directional
B) Cardioid
C) A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array
D) A figure-eight end-fire along the axis of the array
notes.back: A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pair is directional, not omnidirectional. B: a cardioid needs quarter-wave spacing and 90-degree phasing. D: the end-fire figure-eight is the 180-degree case.
notes.explanation: Fed in phase, the pair radiates most broadside to the line joining the verticals, in a figure-eight.
notes.evidence: wavelength apart and fed in phase? A. Omni-directional B. Cardioid C. A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array

notes.front: What happens to the radiation pattern of an unterminated long wire antenna as the wire length is increased?
notes.choices:
A) Fewer lobes form with the major lobes increasing closer to broadside to the wire
B) Additional lobes form with major lobes increasingly aligned with the axis of the antenna
C) The elevation angle increases, and the front-to-rear ratio decreases
D) The elevation angle increases, while the front-to-rear ratio is unaffected
notes.back: Additional lobes form with major lobes increasingly aligned with the axis of the antenna
notes.choicesExplained: A: lengthening adds lobes rather than removing them. C and D: the change is in the number and direction of the lobes, not a rising elevation angle.
notes.explanation: The major lobes swing towards the line of the wire as it lengthens; the Navy course adds that long wires concentrate radiation at low vertical angles.
notes.evidence: What happens to the radiation pattern of an unterminated long wire antenna as the wire length is increased?

notes.front: What is the purpose of feeding an off-center-fed dipole (OCFD) between the center and one end instead of at the midpoint?
notes.choices:
A) To create a similar feed point impedance on multiple bands
B) To suppress off-center lobes at higher frequencies
C) To resonate the antenna across a wider range of frequencies
D) To reduce common-mode current coupling on the feed line shield
notes.back: To create a similar feed point impedance on multiple bands
notes.choicesExplained: B: the aim is not to suppress lobes. C: the antenna still resonates on particular bands; the point of the off-centre feed is the impedance. D: reducing common-mode current is not the purpose the pool gives.
notes.explanation: It makes the dipole usable as a multiband antenna: the feed-point impedance is similar on several bands.
notes.evidence: What is the purpose of feeding an off-center-fed dipole (OCFD) between the center and one end instead of at the midpoint?

notes.front: What is the effect of adding a terminating resistor to a rhombic or long-wire antenna?
notes.choices:
A) It reflects the standing waves on the antenna elements back to the transmitter
B) It changes the radiation pattern from bidirectional to unidirectional
C) It changes the radiation pattern from horizontal to vertical polarization
D) It decreases the ground loss
notes.back: It changes the radiation pattern from bidirectional to unidirectional
notes.choicesExplained: A: the resistor absorbs energy rather than reflecting it. C: it does not change the polarization. D: it does not reduce ground loss.
notes.explanation: The Navy course terminates its rhombic in a noninductive resistor precisely to produce a unidirectional pattern.
notes.evidence: What is the effect of adding a terminating resistor to a rhombic or long-wire antenna?

notes.front: What is the approximate feed point impedance at the center of a two-wire half-wave folded dipole antenna?
notes.choices:
A) 300 ohms
B) 72 ohms
C) 50 ohms
D) 450 ohms
notes.back: 300 ohms
notes.choicesExplained: B: 72 ohms is close to a simple dipole's value. C: 50 ohms is a coax impedance, not this antenna's. D: 450 ohms is too high for two conductors.
notes.explanation: Folded-dipole impedance rises as the square of the number of conductors, so two wires give four times a simple dipole's 73 ohms: roughly 300.
notes.evidence: What is the approximate feed point impedance at the center of a two-wire half-wave folded dipole antenna?

notes.front: What is a folded dipole antenna?
notes.choices:
A) A dipole one-quarter wavelength long
B) A center-fed dipole with the ends folded down 90 degrees at the midpoint of each side
C) A half-wave dipole with an additional parallel wire connecting its two ends
D) A dipole configured to provide forward gain
notes.back: A half-wave dipole with an additional parallel wire connecting its two ends
notes.choicesExplained: A: a quarter-wave length is not what defines it. B: folding the ends down adds no parallel conductor. D: its directional characteristics are the same as a simple dipole's.
notes.explanation: The extra conductor runs parallel to the dipole, a small fraction of a wavelength away, and is joined across its ends.
notes.evidence: What is a folded dipole antenna?

notes.front: Which of the following describes a G5RV antenna?
notes.choices:
A) A wire antenna center-fed through a specific length of open-wire line connected to a balun and coaxial feed line
B) A multi-band trap antenna
C) A phased array antenna consisting of multiple loops
D) A wide band dipole using shorted coaxial cable for the radiating elements and fed with a 4:1 balun
notes.back: A wire antenna center-fed through a specific length of open-wire line connected to a balun and coaxial feed line
notes.choicesExplained: B: a trap antenna uses traps, not a set length of open-wire line. C: it is one centre-fed wire, not an array of loops. D: it does not use shorted coax as radiating elements.
notes.explanation: The specific length of open-wire line is part of the design; a balun then joins it to the coaxial feed line.
notes.evidence: Which of the following describes a G5RV antenna?

notes.front: Which of the following describes a Zepp antenna?
notes.choices:
A) A horizontal array capable of quickly changing the direction of maximum radiation by changing phasing lines
B) An end-fed half-wavelength dipole
C) An omni-directional antenna commonly used for satellite communications
D) A vertical array capable of quickly changing the direction of maximum radiation by changing phasing lines
notes.back: An end-fed half-wavelength dipole
notes.choicesExplained: A and D describe arrays steered by changing phasing lines. C: a Zepp is a wire dipole, not a satellite antenna.
notes.explanation: Feeding the half-wave dipole at one end, not in the centre, is what defines the Zepp.
notes.evidence: Which of the following describes a Zepp antenna?

notes.front: How is the far-field elevation pattern of a vertically polarized antenna affected by being mounted over seawater versus soil?
notes.choices:
A) Radiation at low angles decreases
B) Additional lobes appear at higher elevation angles
C) Separate elevation lobes will combine into a single lobe
D) Radiation at low angles increases
notes.back: Radiation at low angles increases
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is the other way round. B and C: the pool's answer is stronger low-angle radiation, not new high lobes or merged lobes.
notes.explanation: Over seawater rather than soil, a vertically polarized antenna sends more of its far-field radiation at low elevation angles.
notes.evidence: How is the far-field elevation pattern of a vertically polarized antenna affected by being mounted over seawater versus soil?

notes.front: Which of the following describes an extended double Zepp antenna?
notes.choices:
A) An end-fed full-wave dipole antenna
B) A center-fed 1.5-wavelength dipole antenna
C) A center-fed 1.25-wavelength dipole antenna
D) An end-fed 2-wavelength dipole antenna
notes.back: A center-fed 1.25-wavelength dipole antenna
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are end-fed; the extended double Zepp is centre-fed. B: 1.5 wavelengths is longer than its 1.25.
notes.explanation: Unlike the end-fed Zepp, it is fed in the centre, and its overall length is one and a quarter wavelengths.
notes.evidence: Which of the following describes an extended double Zepp antenna?

notes.front: How does the radiation pattern of a horizontally polarized antenna vary with increasing height above ground?
notes.choices:
A) The takeoff angle of the lowest elevation lobe increases
B) The takeoff angle of the lowest elevation lobe decreases
C) The horizontal beamwidth increases
D) The horizontal beamwidth decreases
notes.back: The takeoff angle of the lowest elevation lobe decreases
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is the reverse: the angle falls as height rises. C and D: height changes the elevation pattern, not the horizontal beamwidth.
notes.explanation: The lowest elevation lobe carries the lowest-angle radiation; a higher horizontal antenna brings that lobe nearer the horizon.
notes.evidence: How does the radiation pattern of a horizontally polarized antenna vary with increasing height above ground?

notes.front: How does the radiation pattern of a horizontally-polarized antenna mounted above a long slope compare with the same antenna mounted above flat ground?
notes.choices:
A) The main lobe takeoff angle increases in the downhill direction
B) The main lobe takeoff angle decreases in the downhill direction
C) The horizontal beamwidth decreases in the downhill direction
D) The horizontal beamwidth increases in the uphill direction
notes.back: The main lobe takeoff angle decreases in the downhill direction
notes.choicesExplained: A: downhill the takeoff angle falls, not rises. C and D: the pool's answer is a change of takeoff angle, not of horizontal beamwidth.
notes.explanation: Looking downhill, the main lobe leaves at a lower takeoff angle than it would over flat ground.
notes.evidence: How does the radiation pattern of a horizontally-polarized antenna mounted above a long slope compare with the same antenna mounted above flat ground?

notes.front: How much does the gain of an ideal parabolic reflector antenna increase when the operating frequency is doubled?
notes.choices:
A) 2 dB
B) 3 dB
C) 4 dB
D) 6 dB
notes.back: 6 dB
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are too small: 6 dB, a factor of four in power, is the ideal rise.
notes.explanation: Doubling the frequency ideally quadruples a dish's gain, and a factor of four is 6 dB.
notes.evidence: How much does the gain of an ideal parabolic reflector antenna increase when the operating frequency is doubled?

notes.front: How can two linearly polarized Yagi antennas be used to produce circular polarization?
notes.choices:
A) Stack two Yagis to form an array with the respective elements in parallel planes fed 90 degrees out of phase
B) Stack two Yagis to form an array with the respective elements in parallel planes fed in phase
C) Arrange two Yagis on the same axis and perpendicular to each other with the driven elements at the same point on the boom and fed 90 degrees out of phase
D) Arrange two Yagis collinear to each other with the driven elements fed 180 degrees out of phase
notes.back: Two Yagis on the same axis, perpendicular to each other, driven elements at the same point on the boom, fed 90 degrees out of phase
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: with both Yagis' elements in parallel planes, the two share one polarization. D: collinear Yagis fed 180 degrees apart also share one polarization.
notes.explanation: Crossed elements at the same point on the boom, fed a quarter-cycle (90 degrees) apart, combine into circular polarization.
notes.evidence: How can two linearly polarized Yagi antennas be used to produce circular polarization?

notes.front: What is the most efficient location for a loading coil on an electrically short whip?
notes.choices:
A) Near the center of the vertical radiator
B) As low as possible on the vertical radiator
C) At a voltage maximum
D) At a voltage null
notes.back: Near the center of the vertical radiator
notes.choicesExplained: B: low on the radiator is not the most efficient spot the pool gives. C and D: the pool places it by position on the whip, not at a voltage maximum or null.
notes.explanation: Neither the base nor a voltage point is the pool's answer; the coil works best part-way up, near the middle of the radiator.
notes.evidence: What is the most efficient location for a loading coil on an electrically short whip?

notes.front: Why should antenna loading coils have a high ratio of reactance to resistance?
notes.choices:
A) To swamp out harmonics
B) To lower the radiation angle
C) To maximize efficiency
D) To minimize the Q
notes.back: To maximize efficiency
notes.choicesExplained: A: the coil is not a harmonic filter. B: it does not set the radiation angle. D: a high ratio means high Q, not low.
notes.explanation: A high reactance-to-resistance ratio is a high Q, meaning little resistance in the coil to waste power.
notes.evidence: Why should antenna loading coils have a high ratio of reactance to resistance?

notes.front: Approximately how long is a Yagi’s driven element?
notes.choices:
A) 234 divided by frequency in MHz
B) 1005 divided by frequency in MHz
C) 1/4 wavelength
D) 1/2 wavelength
notes.back: 1/2 wavelength
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are formulas, not the approximate length the pool keys. C: a quarter wave is only half that length.
notes.explanation: The Navy course notes the basic element of an array is generally a dipole, sometimes a little longer or shorter than a half wave.
notes.evidence: Approximately how long is a Yagi’s driven element?

notes.front: What happens to SWR bandwidth when one or more loading coils are used to resonate an electrically short antenna?
notes.choices:
A) It is increased
B) It is decreased
C) It is unchanged if the loading coil is located at the feed point
D) It is unchanged if the loading coil is located at a voltage maximum point
notes.back: It is decreased
notes.choicesExplained: A: loading narrows the bandwidth. C and D: the pool gives no coil position that leaves it unchanged.
notes.explanation: Loaded short antennas have a narrow SWR bandwidth, just as higher antenna Q narrows it.
notes.evidence: What happens to SWR bandwidth when one or more loading coils are used to resonate an electrically short antenna?

notes.front: What is an advantage of top loading an electrically short HF vertical antenna?
notes.choices:
A) Lower Q
B) Greater structural strength
C) Higher losses
D) Improved radiation efficiency
notes.back: Improved radiation efficiency
notes.choicesExplained: A: lower Q is not the advantage the pool gives. B: top loading is not about strength. C: higher losses would be a drawback, not an advantage.
notes.explanation: The pool credits top loading of a short HF vertical with improved radiation efficiency.
notes.evidence: What is an advantage of top loading an electrically short HF vertical antenna?

notes.front: What happens as the Q of an antenna increases?
notes.choices:
A) SWR bandwidth increases
B) SWR bandwidth decreases
C) Gain is reduced
D) More common-mode current is present on the feed line
notes.back: SWR bandwidth decreases
notes.choicesExplained: A: the reverse: bandwidth narrows. C: the pool does not tie Q to lower gain. D: common-mode current is not the effect.
notes.explanation: A high-Q antenna, like a high-Q tuned circuit, keeps a good match over a narrower range of frequencies.
notes.evidence: What happens as the Q of an antenna increases?

notes.front: What is the function of a loading coil in an electrically short antenna?
notes.choices:
A) To increase the SWR bandwidth by increasing net reactance
B) To lower the losses
C) To lower the Q
D) To resonate the antenna by cancelling the capacitive reactance
notes.back: To resonate the antenna by cancelling the capacitive reactance
notes.choicesExplained: A: loading coils decrease SWR bandwidth, and the coil cancels reactance rather than adding it. B: the coil adds some loss of its own. C: narrower bandwidth means higher Q, not lower.
notes.explanation: A short antenna is resonant above the operating frequency and so looks capacitive; the coil's inductive reactance cancels that.
notes.evidence: What is the function of a loading coil in an electrically short antenna?

notes.front: How does radiation resistance of a base-fed whip antenna change below its resonant frequency?
notes.choices:
A) Radiation resistance increases
B) Radiation resistance decreases
C) Radiation resistance becomes imaginary
D) Radiation resistance does not depend on frequency
notes.back: Radiation resistance decreases
notes.choicesExplained: A: it falls, not rises. C: radiation resistance does not become imaginary. D: it does depend on frequency.
notes.explanation: Below resonance the whip is electrically shorter than it needs to be, and the pool keys a falling radiation resistance.
notes.evidence: How does radiation resistance of a base-fed whip antenna change below its resonant frequency?

notes.front: Why do most two-element Yagis with normal spacing have a reflector instead of a director?
notes.choices:
A) Lower SWR
B) Higher receiving directivity factor
C) Greater front-to-side
D) Higher gain
notes.back: Higher gain
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the pool's reason is gain, not SWR or front-to-side. B: receiving directivity factor is a receiving-antenna measure.
notes.explanation: With normal spacing, a driven element plus a reflector gives more gain than a driven element plus a director.
notes.evidence: Why do most two-element Yagis with normal spacing have a reflector instead of a director?

notes.front: What is the purpose of making a Yagi’s parasitic elements either longer or shorter than resonance?
notes.choices:
A) Wind torque cancellation
B) Mechanical balance
C) Control of phase shift
D) Minimize losses
notes.back: Control of phase shift
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: element length is not set for wind or balance. D: the aim is phase control, not loss reduction.
notes.explanation: The phase of the current in a parasitic element depends on its length: the Navy course makes a reflector electrically inductive, a little longer than resonance, so its re-radiated signal adds forward and cancels behind.
notes.evidence: What is the purpose of making a Yagi’s parasitic elements either longer or shorter than resonance?
